title: Maps and routing
like: a maps app like Google Maps
brief: You run a maps app with places, routes and live traffic. Map pictures never change much, but route lookups, place search and traffic from moving phones do. Soon a whole new continent will start using it. Keep maps fast everywhere without paying to serve the same picture twice.

clarify.q: How fresh must map pictures be?
clarify.a: Map tiles change maybe once a day. A tile can be kept for hours or longer.
About a minute. Phones on the road send speed pings, and the app uses the latest average per road.

clarify.q: Can a route be reused for another person?
clarify.a: Popular routes can. Many people ask for the same commute, so route answers are worth keeping for a few minutes.
Half in North America and a third in Europe today. After the new-continent launch, a big share will be in Asia Pacific.

notes: Reads are map tiles (about 85 percent) and route or place-card lookups (about 15 percent). A tile is about 4 KB here (approx.).
Map imagery for the world is on the order of 80 TB at several zoom levels (approx.).

numbers.label: Tile and route reads per second at peak
Reads that reach your servers with a 95% CDN hit rate
Traffic pings per second at peak

hints: Most requests ask for a picture that was the same yesterday. Where is the cheapest place to keep a copy near the user?
A CDN with a very long keep time serves tiles. When the cache empties, make one request refill each item instead of thousands. For a new continent, send users to the nearest region with geo DNS.
Moving tiles alone cannot remove cross-region route computation. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Maps are mostly a caching problem. Seven in ten requests are for pictures that rarely change, which a CDN serves from near the user. The hard parts are what the CDN cannot do: live traffic from phones, place search and the day the cache is empty.

designs.name: CDN first, two regions behind it
designs.why: A CDN with a one-day keep time and collapsed misses serves nearly all tiles. Geo DNS sends other requests to the nearest of two regions, so launch traffic from Asia Pacific is served from Europe or the US with a modest delay instead of falling over. Traffic pings go through a stream processor into a wide-column store.

tradeoffs: A one-day tile keep time makes the CDN bill small and means a fixed map error can take up to a day to disappear, unless you purge it.
Collapsing misses protects the origin when the cache empties, and makes the first few viewers of each tile wait together.
Serving Asia Pacific from far-away regions is cheap and adds about 150 to 170 ms to every request that is not cached. A third region fixes that for about $5,000 a month.
Live traffic uses eventual consistency. A speed from 60 seconds ago is good enough for routing.
The CDN is the largest line on the bill because it is paid per request and per byte; it is also what keeps the other lines small.
editorial.realWorld: Map apps serve billions of tile requests a day, and over 90 percent come from caches near the user (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Maps and routing: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Separate reusable map tiles from versioned routes and fresh traffic. Version boundaries prevent mixed topology during publication. Traffic and map data have different lifetimes. Moving tiles alone cannot remove cross-region route computation.

fields.label: Step 1. A road tile is updated while old tiles are cached. What identifies a consistent map?
options: Versioned tiles and a compatible map manifest
Overwrite every tile under the same permanent name
fields.explanation: Version boundaries prevent mixed topology during publication.

fields.label: Step 2. Congestion changes after a route was cached. What may be reused?
options: The full route forever because tiles are immutable
Static geometry separately from traffic-dependent route cost, with bounded freshness
fields.explanation: Traffic and map data have different lifetimes.

fields.label: Step 3. A new continent launches. Which latency must be budgeted?
options: User round trips plus synchronous routing and traffic dependencies in their actual regions
fields.explanation: Moving tiles alone cannot remove cross-region route computation.

correctness.responsibility: Separate reusable map tiles from versioned routes and fresh traffic.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
